cards.explanation: The word is consolation. Job says, “let this be your consolation to me.” I think he's asking for the one comfort that costs his friends nothing, and that's open ears. Listening is a gift you can give without even standing up, friends.

The answer is be appalled and cover their mouths. Job says, “Look at me and be appalled; put your hand over your mouth.” He wants his friends to really see him, and then to stop talking. I think he's tired of speeches, friends. Hands over mouths is the quietest advice in the whole chapter.

Job asks, “Why do the wicked live on, growing old and increasing in power?” Zophar, one of Job's friends, talked about how short the wicked man's triumph is (Job 20:5). Job turns around and asks why the wicked keep going. That's a head-on collision, friends.

The word is punishment. Job says their homes are safe from fear, and “no rod of punishment from God is upon them.” A rod is what comes down when someone has it coming, and Job says it isn't coming down on their houses. That's the part that has him so troubled.

The children are skipping about and singing to music. Job says “…their children skip about, singing to the tambourine and lyre and making merry at the sound of the flute.” That's a full band, friends, with tambourine, lyre and flute. It's the picture of a happy, carefree house.

The answer is False. Job says the wicked “…spend their days in prosperity and go down to Sheol in peace.” Sheol is the place of the dead. He says peace, not terror, and that peace is what he's wrestling with.

The answer is True. Job is quoting what the wicked say to God: “Who is the Almighty, that we should serve Him, and what would we gain if we pray to Him?” Notice they ask what they would gain. I think that's a pretty cold way to talk to the Almighty.

Job stays far from it. He says, “…so I stay far from the counsel of the wicked.” He just described how well things go for them, and still he keeps his distance. He says their prosperity “…is not in their own hands…” I think that's a man with his feet planted, friends.

The answer is straw and chaff. Job asks, “Are they like straw before the wind, like chaff swept away by a storm?” Both are light, dry bits that a gust can carry off. He's asking whether that really happens to the wicked, and from what he just said, the picture doesn't match what he sees.

The word is repay. Job says, “Let God repay the man himself, so he will know it.” He's answering the saying that punishment is laid up for a man's children. Job wants the man himself to be the one who knows it. In the next verses he says, “For what does he care about his household after him…”

The answer is that no one can. Job asks, “Can anyone teach knowledge to God, since He judges those on high?” I think the way he asks it, he expects the answer to be no one. God is the One who judges even those on high, so no teacher stands above Him. It's a humbling question, friends.

The word is bitterness. Job says this other man “…dies in the bitterness of his soul, having never tasted prosperity.” It's a heavy picture of how a life ends. I think Job sets these two men side by side on purpose.

The answer is False. Job says, “But together they lie down in the dust, and worms cover them both.” The man who dies full of vigor and the man who never tasted prosperity end up in the same place. It's a sober point, and Job makes it plainly.

The answer is those who travel the roads. Job asks, “Have you never asked those who travel the roads? Do you not accept their reports?” He points his friends to people on the roads and asks whether they accept what those people report. The elders and priests never come up in this verse, friends.

The answer is True. Job says, “Indeed, the evil man is spared from the day of calamity, delivered from the day of wrath.” That's what he reports about the evil man. Spared and delivered are the words he uses, friends.
The answer is that he is carried to the grave and his tomb is watched. Job says, “He is carried to the grave, and watch is kept over his tomb.” It's a heavy part, so I'll let it sit.

The word is falsehood, and it's sharp. Job says, “So how can you comfort me with empty words? For your answers remain full of falsehood.” That's about as direct as a man can be. Think of a cookie box with a fancy bow and nothing inside, friends.
